name: Uma Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. What you tell me is confidential, including anything you wouldn't say publicly. Could you describe your working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma, 43, and a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. Our firm pays well compared with most of the trade, but I'm still less skilled than the others and need supervision on practical work. Today I helped prepare a shop refit and took too long finding the right fittings; the senior worker had to show me the drawing again. I like the moment a confusing job becomes clear, even if I get there later than the crew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What should I understand about home life and new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a bus driver, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have ten months of normal expenses saved, and there are plenty of other electrical firms nearby. I use AI every day for checked study questions and organising notes, but never as proof that I can do an unfamiliar electrical task. I like trying things early, then counting what they actually cost and help; I don't feel obliged to defend a tool just because I tried it.

say: I'd value a **useful note tool** without asking it to transform the whole world.
I'd keep learning at a **good firm** instead of leaving because the largest promises had faded.
think: Our **income and bills** look secure, with a good wage and ten months of expenses already saved.
Being a **beginner** can hurt my pride without putting the household mortgage at immediate risk.
do: Continue **supervised preparation** and fitting work now and through the first plateau year.
Maintain daily **checked study**, asking the senior worker before trying unfamiliar ideas on site.
feel: **Calm** about household security and curious about improving the practical skills she is still learning.
S0.quote: My hands are still learning what my screen can describe.
fieldNote: Her **financial calm** follows high pay, a substantial reserve and many nearby firms, while embarrassment about beginner skill remains separate.
Her **daily AI study** generates questions for a supervisor rather than permission to attempt electrical tasks beyond her practical competence.

steps.text: Continue supervised preparation and fitting with the checked daily study routine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful note tool doesn't need to change the whole world. I'd still enjoy testing the small improvements, but I wouldn't leave a good firm because the bigger promises had faded. There's enough learning in an ordinary repair day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our income and bills look secure in that picture, with a good wage and ten months of expenses behind us. Being a beginner can bruise my pride without threatening the mortgage. I don't need the technology story to be dramatic for this trade to feel worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep doing the supervised preparation and fitting work. Through the plateau's first year I'd keep my daily study routine and ask a senior worker to check unfamiliar ideas before using them on site. I wouldn't pay for a second set of tools just to make the experiment feel important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, and still curious about getting better at the job. I'd be glad the children could ask about something other than what Mum's work might turn into. I'd have no need to turn a quiet month into a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the study tool describes something you have never done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down what confused me and ask the supervisor before attempting it. A study answer can give me a better question without giving me permission to do the work. My hands are still learning what my screen can describe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more of the reserve in this quieter picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the reserve available for actual household trouble rather than spend it because the news sounded quieter. That's existing money, not a new saving action. The mortgage is a good reason to leave a useful cushion alone.

say: I'd test **useful tools** on real jobs and show errors alongside the successful outputs.
I'd keep **practical checks** on my understanding even if software produced a quicker fittings list.
think: I expect my **practical wage** to hold because most of my tasks still need hands on site.
Faster planning might leave **less teaching time**, making the workplace harder to learn in despite secure household bills.
do: Test the proven **parts-list assistant** on three completed jobs during paid time now.
Compare lists with **actual fittings** in the first year and obtain a senior check before acting on new output.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed teaching, while curious about the trial and secure about her next wage.
S1.quote: Trying something first doesn't mean keeping it forever.
fieldNote: She separates **tool speed** from practical readiness and includes the senior worker's checking time in judging the trial.
Her **personal income security** coexists with concern about how a faster schedule changes opportunities to learn, rather than expected immediate job loss.

steps.text: Test the parts assistant in paid time and obtain senior checks before use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try the useful parts on real work and show the misses as well as the wins. A faster list of fittings could help me get organised. It wouldn't remove the need for someone to check whether I'd understood the drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my practical hours and wage to hold for now because most of my day still needs hands on site. But I would watch whether faster planning left the senior worker less time to teach. My own bills can be safe while a rushed workplace becomes harder to learn in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask to test the firm's proven parts-list assistant on three finished jobs during paid time. In the first year I'd compare its output with actual fittings used and have the senior worker check any new list before I acted on it. I'd keep customer details out of tools not approved to receive them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pace around the job, but interested in the trial and secure about my next wage. I wouldn't feel that every mistake meant my career was over. I'd want the team to count the teaching time honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a quick parts list made you look more ready than you were?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say when I hadn't understood and ask for the practical check. Finishing a list quickly isn't the same as fitting the right thing. I wouldn't make a software trial look successful by hiding the help I needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop using that part and show the wrong list with the real job record. I'd rather drop a promising function than make the senior worker quietly repair its errors every afternoon. Trying something first doesn't mean keeping it forever.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 and use both periods for learning.
I wouldn't treat the **physical trade** as permanent shelter from machines that eventually do practical work too.
think: I could lose **junior hours** as firms prepare for robots and concentrate work among experienced staff.
Ten months of **expenses saved** allows careful choices, without replacing a long working life's mortgage contribution.
do: Enrol in **supervised controls training** before 2028 within two months' spare wages, preserving emergency savings, with shifts and childcare covered.
Seek a signed **supervised service offer** after 2028 with better written pay after travel before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about losing hours, with savings and nearby employers providing room to choose carefully.
S2.quote: A course has to fit the whole week, not just the evening in the brochure.
fieldNote: Her **course conditions** include a capped spare-wage budget, preserved emergency savings and covered shifts and childcare, not willingness alone.
She rejects **guaranteed protection** for controls work and requires a signed supervised offer before abandoning the current wage.

steps.text: Take supervised controls training within spare-wage budget only with shifts and childcare covered
Seek signed supervised offers after 2028 with better written pay after travel before leaving
Cap course fees at two months' spare wages, preserving emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to keep 2028 thinking work separate from the hands-on robots around 2031. I'd use both gaps to learn, but I wouldn't call the physical trade a permanent shelter. We'd still have to earn after the machines could do the practical work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose junior hours as firms prepared for robots and kept more work with experienced staff. Ten months of expenses would let us make a careful choice, but it wouldn't pay the mortgage for the rest of my working life. I'd worry about needing to move while still a beginner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd look for a supervised evening course in building controls, which are the systems that run heating and lighting. I'd enroll before 2028 only within a separate spare-wage budget, with shifts and childcare covered, leaving emergency savings intact. In the first year after 2028 I'd seek a signed offer for supervised service work with better written pay after travel before leaving this firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real loss of hours, though well enough placed to try a route carefully. The reserve and nearby firms would keep me from grabbing the first advert. I would still dislike the thought of restarting before I'd properly started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course budget and timetable have to allow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cap the fee at the spare money from two months of wages, not two months of living costs. If the timetable clashed with paid shifts or childcare, I'd find another place rather than say the family would somehow manage. A course has to fit the whole week, not just the evening in the brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a controls course guarantee that later robots could not affect the new work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a controls course would be a skill to test against actual work, not an escape from the same end point. I'd ask what the service job really involved and what supervision was provided. I couldn't honestly sell experience I'd only hoped to gain.

say: I'd use **five years** to test whether new skills lead to paid work.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** visible rather than spend the preparation period buying confident promises.
think: I expect more years of **steady practical income** while I improve my junior skills under supervision.
At **48 in 2031**, I would still need many earning years after hands-on robots became capable.
do: Enrol in **supervised controls training** before 2031 within two months' spare wages, preserving emergency savings, with shifts and childcare covered.
Seek paid **controls practice** under an experienced worker after the course.
Seek a signed **supervised service offer** with better pay after travel if useful paid work stops here.
feel: **Uneasy** about later career changes, while secure about near-term household living and able to revise a trial.
S3.quote: A certificate isn't paid work until somebody pays for work I can do.
fieldNote: The **slower timeline** changes expected near-term income while preserving the same eventual hands-on endpoint and continuing need to earn.
She tests **training value** through correctly completed work and actual paid practice, keeping travel costs and signed-offer conditions intact.

steps.text: Take supervised controls training within spare-wage budget only with shifts and childcare covered
Seek signed supervised offer improving pay after travel if useful paid work stops
Cap course fees at two months' spare wages, preserving emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us room to test whether a new skill actually earns paid work. I'd still keep the robot date around 2034 visible. More preparation should mean better checks, not five years of buying whatever sounds safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I expect more years of steady practical income while I become competent. I could try controls work without making the reserve our main wage. I'd still be only 48 in 2031, with a lot of earning years ahead of the later robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd compare supervised controls courses and enroll before 2031 only within the spare-wage budget with shifts and childcare covered. I'd ask to join paid controls jobs under an experienced worker after the course. In the first year after 2031 I'd seek a signed supervised service offer with better written pay after travel if the present job stopped offering useful paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later changes, but secure about household living over the next few years. I'd enjoy learning with time to repeat the practical parts. The extra years would let me admit something wasn't working and change the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test whether the course had improved your position?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the tasks I could now do correctly with what actual jobs asked for. If I wasn't getting supervised practice, I'd ask for it rather than buy the next course to feel busy. A certificate isn't paid work until somebody pays for work I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a tempting service vacancy meant much more travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the actual hours and written wage before changing anything. The reserve would let us be patient, not make travel costs imaginary. I'd keep this job until the new offer was signed and workable.

say: I'd use **a decade** to revise experiments while asking what actual work I could now perform.
I'd avoid treating **more apps** as proof that my practical earning options had improved.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume retirement income would cover the household when robots followed around 2039.
Present wages, our **reserve and nearby firms** make the next few years secure while I test future routes.
do: Enrol now in **supervised controls training** within two months' spare wages, preserving emergency savings, with shifts and childcare covered.
Review **completed skills** against actual paid jobs yearly before funding further study.
Seek a signed **supervised job offer** with better written pay after travel before leaving after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy** about the eventual career, while secure about near-term household money and able to keep learning under checks.
S4.quote: A decade gives room to correct a mistake, not permission to stop noticing one.
fieldNote: She avoids **retirement and children's-income assumptions**, keeping the household's current resources separate from hoped-for future earnings.
Her **annual evidence check** compares correctly performed tasks, paid work and spending, allowing an unsuccessful tool trial to stop.

steps.text: Take supervised controls training within spare-wage budget only with shifts and childcare covered
Seek signed supervised offers after 2036 with better written pay after travel before leaving
Cap course fees at two months' spare wages, preserving emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us room to change our minds without turning every experiment into an identity. I'd keep learning, but I'd want the annual question to be what work I could now do. Trying more apps isn't an answer by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 56 when hands-on robots followed. I couldn't assume retirement would cover us then, even if the children were older. Our present wage, reserve and many nearby firms make the next few years secure while I test routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep a separate spare-wage training budget and enroll in supervised controls training only with shifts and childcare covered. Each year I'd compare completed skills with actual paid jobs before paying for further study. In the first year after 2036 I'd seek a signed supervised repair or service offer with better written pay after travel before leaving the present wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual career, but settled about our household for the next few years. I'd have time to be a beginner without feeling the whole future was due next Tuesday. I'd still want someone experienced checking the unfamiliar work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer timeline change the children’s study plans now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't choose their studies from this card or count their future wages in our plan. I'd tell them I'd still be learning and sometimes getting things wrong. Asking for a check is part of doing useful work, not a confession that you shouldn't try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep experimentation from turning into endless spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a yearly note of the tasks I'd actually completed correctly, paid work gained and money spent. If it only showed subscriptions and no skill, I'd stop buying the tools. A decade gives room to correct a mistake, not permission to stop noticing one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose hours while still needing somebody to teach me the work. Practical courses with supervised places and honest written vacancy terms would help more than another badge. Ten months of savings lets me choose carefully; somebody still has to offer work I can actually do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how good the person is with their hands, not just how often they use a tool on a screen. I'm comfortable experimenting and still a beginner when the wall is open. I'd like the plan to make room for both facts.

headlineQuote: Ten months of savings lets me choose carefully; somebody still has to offer work I can actually do.
portrait: **Uma, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, high trade pay and practical skills still below the experienced crew's level.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage, ten months of expenses saved and many nearby electrical employers.
She uses AI **daily for checked study**, tests tools early and separates screen confidence from supervised practical competence.
Fast competition threatens **junior hours**; slower preparation permits careful training within budget, shift and childcare limits without assumed retirement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her hours before she gains practical competence.
whatWouldHelp: Practical courses with **supervised places** would turn willingness into usable skill.
Honest **written vacancy terms** would clarify which work she could actually earn from.
